passes.notes: Both answers recommend free, legible families and give a sensible self-hosted WOFF2 setup with a fallback stack ending in sans-serif. A is stronger on device testing: it tells the reader to try an old Android phone, a library computer and a cheap test print. B only suggests blocking the font in a browser and checking glyphs, and its repeated doubts about whether Source Sans 3 is under the SIL Open Font License (it is) weaken an otherwise clear single-family answer that ties web and print together well.

Answer A gives a clear plan for one family across web and print, with ready CSS. However, it hedges on a license that is in fact OFL and never suggests testing on a real old phone, a library PC or a test print. Answer B is accurate about licensing and tells the user to check on real devices and a cheap printer. Its body-font advice is a little split between print and web, and it says library PCs fall back to Arial when system-ui would pick Segoe UI first.
